newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: YEAREND-Malaysia stocks seen at all-time high in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Malaysia stocks seen at all-time high in '97.

text.p: After a 20 percent rise in 1996, Malaysia's blue-chip share index is expected to hit an all-time high in the coming year, led by banking, construction and infrastructure stocks, analysts said on Monday.
They said after a year of much needed economic moderation, which saw Malaysia's worrisome external balances improving, macro-economic factors would take a back seat in 1997.
Instead, share prices would be led by outlook for individual industries, they added.
"Trade (deficit) will be a non-issue in 1997," said Simon Maughan, head of research at stockbrokers W.I. Carr Malaysia.
Maughan predicted that the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Composite Index would rise to 1,350 during 1997, led by companies in the construction and banking sectors.
The Composite Index is a weighted average of 100 stocks with a minimum paid-up capital of 40 million ringgit.
Analysts said that after the intense speculation driven by merger rumours in 1996, banking stocks would also be in focus next year.

After the announcement of the acquisition of Kwong Yik Bank Bhd by Rashid Hussain Bhd in November, Malaysia's largest institutional stock broker, several other banks have been the subject of merger and takeover rumours.
Many analysts see this trend continuing in 1997, with Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara brokering many deals.
The Composite Index closed on January 5, 1994 at a record high of 1,332.04. But despite several runs since then, the barometer index has remained stubbornly below that level.
The Composite Index has now gained around 20 percent this year from its close of 995.17 on Dec 29, 1995.

"We are anticipating a 19 to 20 percent increase on the index in ringgit terms, and this translates to around 1,428 on the Composite Index by the end of 1997," said John Engle, managing director of the research house H.G. Asia Sdn Bhd.
Engle sees this as being possible on the back of a stable political environment, improvement in Malaysia's trade deficit and a stabilising U.S. dollar/yen exchange rate.

"Over 50 percent of Malaysia's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth comes from private investment in the construction industry. The best proxies to this growth are infrastructure developers," said Maughan of W.I. Carr.

Arnold Lim, general manager of HLG Asset Management in Kuala Lumpur, also feels infrastructure stocks will play a big part in the 1997 rally. "There will be a rush to complete many infastructure projects before the 1998 Commonwealth Games," he said.
However, some see the construction industry as facing some problems over the next two years.

"Some (construction) companies may not get all the potential earnings from their projects in the early years," said Pearlene Cheong, research manager at K.L. Mutual Fund Bhd. "How long will investors support this industry? That is the question."
She also cited a slower increase in the selling prices for luxury commercial properties and the creeping oversupply across the spectrum as contributors to a decline in investor support.
The analysts said among the stocks that are seen to be fundamentally the strongest in 1997 are Gamuda Bhd, Road Builder Holdings, Bolton Properties Bhd and Sungei Way Holdings Bhd.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
